content: The relationship between concentration and mortality is analyzed using log-probit regression, and the LC50 and LC90 values are reported. If mortality in the control group exceeds 20%, the test is invalidated. To assess cross-resistance via known resistance mechanisms, tests should be conducted using well-characterized susceptible and resistant strains. If homozygosity cannot be achieved, periodic selection is necessary to prevent natural selection for susceptible alleles from reducing resistance. Reference strains should be monitored at least twice a year using bioassays or molecular assays to detect, assess, and correct any reversion in resistance through selection. Comparing the LD50 values of susceptible mosquito strains with those of distinct resistant strains provides an estimation of the existence and level of cross-resistance of the candidate insecticide. Cross-resistance is indicated if the LD50 or LD95 of a strain carrying a specific resistance mechanism is significantly higher than that of the corresponding susceptible strain. The biological activity of aerosols intended for rapid action is determined in a Peet-Grady chamber on free-flying mosquitoes. The chamber floor is covered with absorbent white paper, divided into quadrants for easy observation and recording of knocked-down mosquitoes. Fifty non-blood-fed, 2–5-day-old female mosquitoes are released into the chamber. The aerosol container is shaken, placed in an automatic dispenser, and sprayed into a fume hood for 3–5 seconds to prime the dispenser. Ten grams of the formulated product is sprayed in a single application toward the center of the chamber. The number of knocked-down mosquitoes is recorded every minute for 10 minutes and subsequently at 10-minute intervals for a total of 60 minutes. Observers may be assigned to different quadrants for accurate recording. After 60 minutes, the chamber is ventilated, and the knocked-down and remaining mosquitoes are collected with an aspirator and transferred into separate clean holding cups. The mosquitoes are provided with a 10% sugar solution on cotton wool and held for 24 hours at 27°C ± 2°C and 80% ± 10% relative humidity. Mortality is recorded 24 hours after exposure. If mortality in the control group exceeds 20%, the test is invalidated. Aerosols designed for combined rapid action and limited residual activity are evaluated in two steps. First, rapid knock-down and mortality are assessed as described above. Second, residual activity is evaluated by spraying the aerosol onto substrates (e.g., carpet) in the Peet-Grady chamber. One hour after spraying, the substrates are removed and subjected to WHO cone bioassays. Ten non-blood-fed, susceptible female mosquitoes aged 2–5 days are introduced into plastic WHO cones secured to four treated substrates for 30 minutes. The mosquitoes are then transferred into clean cups, provided with a 10% sugar solution, and held for 24 hours at 27°C ± 2°C and 80% ± 10% relative humidity. Knock-down is recorded at 60 minutes, and mortality is recorded after 24 hours. Control bioassays are conducted on untreated substrates in the same manner. If mortality in the control group exceeds 20%, the test is invalidated. Products intended for aircraft disinsection must be tested in realistic settings inside aircraft representative of those used on long-haul international flights. The minimum internal cabin dimensions for testing should be 30 m x 5 m. At least two replicates should be conducted with a susceptible mosquito species, using both singleand dual-aisle seating aircraft. No residual insecticide should have been applied in the aircraft during the previous three months. Baseline testing with appropriate bioassays (control cages or WHO cones) should be performed to ensure no contamination with pesticide residues. Tests are conducted under ambient climatic conditions, with the aircraft climate control maintaining a temperature of 23°C ± 2°C when possible. Ambient temperature and relative humidity are recorded, along with the exact dimensions of the cabin or hold used. For passenger cabins, all toilet doors, garment storage lockers, and overhead luggage compartments should be open, the air-conditioning switched off, and the outer door closed during spraying. The flight deck should not be treated, and its access door should remain closed. Tests are conducted by placing mosquito cages in three areas of the main passenger cabin: the middle row of seats, the fifth row from the front, and the fifth row from the rear. Cylindrical steel-frame cages containing 25 non-blood-fed, 2–5-day-old female mosquitoes are placed on each side of the cabin, with one in the foot space beneath the window seat, another on the bottom cushion of the aisle seat, and a third in the middle of the open overhead luggage compartment. This placement is repeated in the mid, front, and rear of the cabin. Additional cages are placed in at least one toilet area and one galley area. For dual-aisle aircraft, an additional series of cages is placed in the middle seating area at each location, with extra cages in a second toilet and galley area. For cargo holds, mosquito cages are placed singly on clean paper on the floor, 10 cm from each corner of the hold area. Additional cages are hung 10 cm from the ceiling and walls in each corner, with three more evenly spaced along the central axis of the hold at a height of 1 m. The same number of cages is used for a control group. Cage bioassays are conducted by positioning mosquito cages according to the aircraft design and applying the insecticide product as per the manufacturer’s instructions or national procedures. The external door is opened 60 minutes after application, and the area is ventilated before entry. The number of knocked-down mosquitoes is counted, and the cages are removed from the aircraft. The mosquitoes are transferred into clean holding cups, provided with a 10% sugar solution, and held for 24 hours at 27°C ± 2°C and 80% ± 10% relative humidity. The average percentage of knocked-down mosquitoes after 60 minutes and mortality after 24 hours are reported. Control cages are placed at the same locations, held for 60 minutes, and removed from the aircraft. If mortality in the control group exceeds 20%, the test is invalidated. Residual activity is evaluated one hour after application using WHO cone bioassays. Ten non-blood-fed, susceptible female mosquitoes aged 2–5 days are introduced into WHO cones secured to treated surfaces for 30 minutes. The mosquitoes are then transferred into clean holding cups, provided with a 10% sugar solution, and held for 24 hours at 27°C ± 2°C and 80% ± 10% relative humidity. Knock-down is measured at 60 minutes, and mortality is recorded after 24 hours. A minimum of three replicates from separately reared batches are tested per location, and the results are pooled for analysis. Control WHO cone bioassays are conducted in the same manner and at the same locations. If mortality in the control group exceeds 20%, the results of the entire test are rejected.
